# Control-Theoretic Design of an Integrated 3D Crop-Grain Phenotyping System

The recommended design is a modular, closed-loop phenotyping instrument with two operating branches. For external grain morphology, a calibrated structured-light or line-laser stereo system should provide the primary metric measurements; passive multi-view stereo (MVS), structure-from-motion (SfM), or 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) should provide lower-cost and more portable alternatives. X-ray micro-computed tomography (CT) should be added when embryo, endosperm, cavity, density, or other internal traits are required. The acquisition system should be represented by a nonlinear stochastic state-space model and operated through state estimation, constrained model predictive control (MPC), disturbance observation, and, where necessary, adaptive or robust control.

The existing literature demonstrates useful grain-level accuracy, trait extraction, and throughput. For example, structured-light wheat measurements achieved length, width, and thickness MAPE values of 1.83%, 1.86%, and 2.19%, respectively, while a line-laser binocular system reported approximately 12 seconds of scanning and 3.18 seconds of processing per grain. A six-cultivar smartphone-based 3DGS study demonstrated cross-species reconstruction of maize, wheat, and rice seeds, but also showed larger errors for the width and height of slender rice grains. CT systems remain the strongest option for internal anatomy, although scan time, data volume, cost, and segmentation complexity limit routine high-throughput use. These findings support a modality-specific architecture rather than a single universal sensor.

The control-theoretic design proposed here is an engineering synthesis. The supplied crop-grain literature does not provide identified crop-grain process models, validated feedback controllers, or closed-loop stability, controllability, observability, and identifiability benchmarks for grain-imaging loops. Consequently, controller equations, timing budgets, acceptance tests, and experimental specifications below are proposed design elements. They should be treated as hypotheses to be identified and validated experimentally, not as established crop-grain performance results.

## Roadmap

The report first defines the phenotyping problem and the design criteria that connect metric accuracy, phenotype completeness, throughput, and robustness. It then specifies an integrated sensing architecture and measurement model spanning sample handling, motion, illumination, image acquisition, reconstruction, segmentation, trait extraction, and quality feedback.

The control section formulates the instrument as a nonlinear stochastic state-space system, explains system identification and Bayesian state estimation, and compares constrained MPC, robust MPC, adaptive robust MPC, and disturbance-observer designs. The reconstruction section then places SfM–MVS, structured light, line-laser stereo, RGB-D, LiDAR, CT, NeRF, and 3DGS within the same inverse-problem framework.

The final sections define a grain-phenotype catalogue, uncertainty and validation procedures, implementation specifications, failure modes, and a research roadmap. Throughout, results measured on wheat, rice, maize, other seeds, whole plants, or transferable control systems are kept distinct from proposed grain-specific designs.

## 1. Research context, objectives, and design criteria

### 1.1 The design problem

A crop-grain phenotyping instrument is not merely a camera followed by a segmentation algorithm. It is a coupled physical and computational system in which sample presentation, object motion, illumination, sensor geometry, camera triggering, calibration, reconstruction, segmentation, and trait computation influence one another.

The object of measurement may be:

- an isolated dry grain on a carrier;
- several grains arranged with controlled spacing;
- a densely packed batch;
- a grain attached to a spike or panicle;
- a kernel whose internal embryo, endosperm, or cavity must be measured; or
- a dynamic sample moving through a conveyor-based inspection system.

These cases have different observability and control requirements. An isolated grain on a matte stage is largely a geometric measurement problem. A packed batch adds instance-separation and occlusion uncertainty. A grain on a moving conveyor introduces motion blur, timing delay, and pose uncertainty. CT adds internal structure but changes the measurement chain, data volume, and throughput.

The design objective is therefore a vector rather than a single accuracy number:

\[
\mathcal{J}=\{A_{\mathrm{metric}},C_{\mathrm{trait}},T_{\mathrm{throughput}},R_{\mathrm{robustness}},B_{\mathrm{calibration}},D_{\mathrm{damage}}\}
\]

where \(A_{\mathrm{metric}}\) is metric accuracy, \(C_{\mathrm{trait}}\) is trait completeness, \(T_{\mathrm{throughput}}\) is useful sample throughput, \(R_{\mathrm{robustness}}\) is performance under disturbances, \(B_{\mathrm{calibration}}\) is calibration burden, and \(D_{\mathrm{damage}}\) represents destructive or invasive effects. No modality optimizes all six terms simultaneously.

The immediate research objective should be stated at the level of a measurable system requirement:

> Estimate a declared set of external and, where applicable, internal grain traits from calibrated 3D data while maintaining specified bounds on bias, repeatability, uncertainty, latency, and failure probability across the intended species, cultivars, moisture states, orientations, packing densities, and illumination conditions.

This formulation prevents an image-quality score from being substituted for phenotype accuracy. A reconstruction may render photorealistic views while still biasing thickness, surface area, curvature, or volume. Conversely, a sparse geometric model may be adequate for length and width while being unsuitable for fine surface descriptors.

### 1.2 From manual measurement to controlled 3D phenotyping

The historical transition is important because each major sensing development solved a different limitation.

Traditional 2D imaging made length, width, projected area, color, and outline measurements inexpensive, but projection confounds true three-dimensional thickness, orientation, and surface area. Agricultural 3D imaging subsequently developed around triangulation, time-of-flight, and interferometric principles. A broad agricultural review identifies stereo vision, MVS, multiple-baseline stereo, SfM, shape-from-silhouette, structured light, shape-from-shading, and shape-from-focus as triangulation-based alternatives, with different calibration and environmental requirements [Vázquez-Arellano et al., *3D imaging systems for agricultural applications*](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/16/5/618).

Active optical methods then improved depth precision by projecting structured light or laser energy. The wheat structured-light system of [Wang et al.](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/plant-science/articles/10.3389/fpls.2022.840908/full) used a black stage, a 30° turntable rotation, and a 37° scan angle as its best tested condition. The reported scanner specification was 0.05 mm single-sided accuracy within 2 seconds, a 0.16 mm point distance, and a 0.05 mm spatial resolution. These are system-specific anchors, not universal settings.

CT introduced a separate transition from surface geometry to volumetric anatomy. It can recover complete cross-sectional stacks and support non-destructive measurement of embryo, endosperm, cavity, density, and internal defects. The 2023 maize-kernel pipeline used 700 tomographic images at 2000 × 2000 pixels and extracted 20 external and internal traits from an individual kernel within 5 seconds after imaging [Li et al., *CT-Based Phenotyping and Genome-Wide Association Analysis of the Internal Structure and Components of Maize Kernels*](https://doi.org/10.3390/agronomy13041078). The scan itself, however, remains a separate cost and throughput constraint.

Neural representations changed the reconstruction stage. NeRF introduced an implicit neural representation for view synthesis, while 3DGS uses explicit anisotropic Gaussian primitives that can be optimized and rendered efficiently. A 2025 seed study used SfM for camera poses and sparse initialization, then optimized Gaussian position, covariance, opacity, and appearance through differentiable rendering. Its authors explicitly identified high-precision seed-scale 3DGS phenotyping as still relatively unexplored [Agriculture (2025), *Seed 3D Phenotyping Across Multiple Crops Using 3D Gaussian Splatting*](https://doi.org/10.3390/agriculture15222329).

The current transition is from open-loop reconstruction toward active sensing. Instead of acquiring a fixed sequence and accepting whatever quality results, the instrument can estimate pose coverage, blur, illumination, and reconstruction uncertainty during acquisition. It can then change conveyor speed, turntable angle, camera position, exposure, focus, or illumination. Digital-twin work in field phenotyping has already articulated a perception–prediction–decision–execution loop, although the reported system was a rail-based field platform rather than an individual-grain controller [DT-FieldPheno](https://doi.org/10.3390/agriculture15111217). The grain-specific research opportunity is to bring this loop into a controlled, measurable instrument.

### 1.3 Design criteria

The design should satisfy the following criteria.

| Criterion | Engineering meaning | Consequence for the system |
|---|---|---|
| Metric validity | Dimensions and derived geometry must be expressed in a calibrated physical coordinate system | Use intrinsic/extrinsic calibration, scale references, and traceable reference objects |
| Trait completeness | The selected modality must expose the surfaces or internal structures needed by the biological question | Use structured light or laser for external traits and CT for internal anatomy |
| Throughput | Acquisition and processing must fit the experimental sample size and conveyor spacing | Use asynchronous reconstruction, event-based quality control, and modality-specific operating modes |
| Robustness | Performance must tolerate motion, illumination drift, occlusion, vibration, and cultivar variation | Estimate disturbances and use constrained robust or adaptive control |
| Biological interpretability | Geometric axes and descriptors must not be confused with anatomical axes or causal traits | Declare axis conventions and combine morphology with cultivar, stress, moisture, and developmental metadata |

The system should also distinguish three evidence levels:

1. **Measured evidence:** reported accuracy, timing, or validation results from a named study.
2. **Transferable theory:** control, estimation, uncertainty, or morphometric methods demonstrated in another system.
3. **Proposed design:** a specification that must be identified and tested in the intended grain instrument.

This distinction is especially important for control. MPC and disturbance observers are well established in robotics and process systems. That does not establish their stability or performance in a crop-grain imaging loop until the relevant states, delays, actuators, and disturbances are identified.

## 2. Integrated sensing architecture and crop-grain measurement model

### 2.1 Reference architecture

The proposed architecture separates physical acquisition, reconstruction, phenotype analysis, and control while allowing feedback between them.

```text
Sample identification and presentation
        │
        ▼
Carrier / turntable / robotic stage ── encoder, limit switch, IMU
        │                         ▲
        ▼                         │
Camera, projector, laser, CT, lighting ── exposure, focus, intensity control
        │
        ▼
Calibration and synchronization
        │
        ▼
Images / disparities / projections / point clouds / CT slices
        │
        ▼
Reconstruction branch
  SfM–MVS | structured light | line laser | RGB-D | 3DGS | CT
        │
        ▼
Denoising, registration, scale recovery, surface or volume reconstruction
        │
        ▼
Instance segmentation and semantic labeling
        │
        ▼
Trait extraction and uncertainty estimation
        │
        ├── phenotype record
        ├── quality and failure flags
        └── reconstruction-confidence feedback
                         │
                         ▼
State estimator ── MPC / robust control / adaptive control
                         │
                         ├── motion command
                         ├── trigger timing
                         ├── illumination
                         ├── focus and exposure
                         └── rescan / reject / stop
```

The architecture should maintain separate records for:

- the biological sample and its metadata;
- raw sensor data;
- calibration parameters and calibration quality;
- reconstructed geometry;
- segmentation masks and instance identities;
- extracted traits;
- uncertainty and quality flags;
- control actions and environmental conditions.

This separation is not bureaucratic. It allows a researcher to determine whether a trait error arose from scale drift, missing geometry, segmentation, mesh closure, biological variation, or the control decision that selected the acquisition condition.

### 2.2 Modality comparison

#### External morphology

| Modality | Representation and principal use | Reported performance anchors | Main strengths | Main limitations |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Structured light | Calibrated disparity or depth point cloud; external surface morphology | Wheat scanner: 0.05 mm single-sided accuracy within 2 s; wheat dimensions MAPE 1.83–2.19% | High metric precision, controlled geometry, effective for isolated grains | Sensitive to ambient light, calibration, shadows, and occlusion; usually requires fixed geometry |
| Line-laser binocular stereo | Laser-line triangulation and stereo point cloud; conveyor inspection | WG-3D: 25 mm/s carrier, approximately 12 s scanning and 3.18 s processing; volume MAPE 4.31% | Strong fit for inline motion and encoder synchronization | Bottom surface may be unobserved; laser visibility and adhered-grain separation are challenging |
| Passive MVS/SfM | Sparse camera poses followed by dense stereo point cloud or mesh | Wheat seed work: approximately 36 images and 20 s for a conventional volume-carving model; three-image neural variant reported approximately 2% relative errors for volume and dimensions | Low hardware cost, color preservation, flexible viewpoint geometry | Requires texture, overlap, stable objects, and substantial computation; scale is ambiguous without a reference |
| 3DGS / NeRF | Explicit Gaussian representation or implicit radiance field; view synthesis and geometry recovery | Six-cultivar 3DGS seed models had SSIM above 0.95 and PSNR between 35 and 37 dB; visual metrics are not trait validation | High visual fidelity, sparse-view and neural-prior extensions, editable explicit representation for 3DGS | Memory and optimization cost; incomplete bottoms and unseen surfaces; visual realism can exceed metric accuracy |
| RGB-D | Direct depth plus RGB, generally for rapid controlled acquisition | RealSense D435i example: 1280 × 720 at 30 Hz and good depth within approximately 1.5 m in plant scenes | Simple, fast, compact, potentially mobile | Grain-scale depth performance depends strongly on working distance, texture, baseline, and lighting; not established by the cited plant results |
| LiDAR / TLS | Direct range point cloud, generally for plant or field structure | Crop reviews report strong field robustness but high equipment cost; near-range resolution may be unsuitable for detached grains without a dedicated scanner | Good field robustness and large-scene coverage | Cost, near-range resolution, payload, calibration, and excessive data volume for small grains |

Structured light and line-laser stereo are the strongest starting points when the central requirement is high-throughput external grain geometry. MVS and 3DGS are attractive when cost, portability, or color information dominates, but their metric performance must be validated trait by trait. RGB-D and general-purpose LiDAR should not be selected solely because they output depth; the relevant question is whether their depth uncertainty is small relative to grain thickness, surface curvature, and the desired biological effect size.

#### Internal structure

| Modality | External morphology | Internal anatomy | Throughput and cost implication | Recommended role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Optical structured light or laser | Strong for visible surfaces | Not available | Fast and comparatively economical | Primary external measurement |
| Passive MVS or 3DGS | Good when texture and coverage are adequate | Not available | Low hardware cost but potentially high computation | Portable screening and visual reconstruction |
| RGB-D | Moderate to strong in controlled working ranges | Not available | Rapid acquisition; grain-scale accuracy requires local testing | Auxiliary sensing or low-cost prototype |
| X-ray CT | Strong if the outer boundary is segmented | Strong; embryo, endosperm, cavities, density-related features | Expensive scans, reconstruction time, memory, and segmentation | Internal-structure reference and selected high-value samples |

CT is not simply a more accurate optical scanner. It measures a different biological object. In the wheat structured-light comparison, structured light had lower \(R^2\) than CT for length, width, and thickness, but similar RMSE and MAPE. Structured-light length, width, and thickness errors were 0.149, 0.076, and 0.080 mm RMSE, compared with CT values of 0.147, 0.086, and 0.082 mm; the structured-light workflow was reported as approximately twice as fast as CT [Frontiers wheat study](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/plant-science/articles/10.3389/fpls.2022.840908/full). The correct conclusion is therefore objective-dependent: CT is superior when internal anatomy matters, whereas optical sensing may provide adequate external dimensions at higher throughput.

### 2.3 Sensor geometry, illumination, and sample motion

#### Geometry

Binocular geometry should be optimized against a stated criterion. One analytical and experimental study found the highest reconstruction accuracy when the angle between the binocular optical axis and baseline was approximately 40°–50°. The same study gave a broader 25°–60° interval for reducing error propagation and recommended a symmetric arrangement with equal left and right angles [Scientific Reports binocular reconstruction study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10557943/). These ranges are not contradictory: the narrower interval optimizes an accuracy measure, whereas the wider interval describes a broader error-propagation criterion.

The study also found that a shorter baseline or longer focal length can reduce measurement error under fixed conditions, but reduced magnification narrows the common field of view. For grain imaging, this creates a direct trade-off between depth precision, coverage, working distance, and depth of field.

Two other angle values should not be confused with the binocular optical-axis angle. The wheat structured-light experiment used a 30° turntable rotation and 37° scanner angle. The cereal-grain structured-light system used eight scans with 45° turntable rotations for a batch of 25 grains. These are acquisition-schedule parameters, not universal stereo-optical specifications.

Placement is also a geometric variable. In a comparison involving rice, wheat, and corn grains, 100 filled rice grains placed vertically produced errors of 2.15%, 0.68%, and 1.18% for length, width, and thickness, compared with 4.55%, 4.05%, and 3.82% under horizontal placement. Horizontal placement produced incomplete point clouds because of scan-angle restrictions [Qin et al.](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-07221-4). A design should therefore either constrain orientation mechanically or measure orientation and include it in the observation model.

#### Illumination

Structured light requires the projected pattern to dominate ambient illumination. A matte black carrier reduces background interference and makes plane removal easier. The wheat structured-light study found a black stage to be part of its best tested condition. Passive MVS requires stable texture and contrast, whereas reflective or nearly textureless grain surfaces can cause sparse features, mismatches, or missing geometry.

A practical enclosure should therefore provide:

- diffuse, spectrally stable illumination for passive color imaging;
- synchronized projector or laser emission for active depth;
- controlled background reflectance;
- shielding from direct sunlight and changing ambient light;
- a brightness and saturation monitor in the image loop; and
- a reference patch or calibration target visible in at least some frames.

The field-phenotyping literature reinforces the importance of environmental control. Structured-light performance can degrade under strong ambient light, while MVS is affected by textureless regions, reflective surfaces, and illumination variation [Agronomy review](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4395/15/11/2518). For a detached-grain instrument, enclosure is usually more effective than trying to make the reconstruction algorithm compensate for uncontrolled illumination.

#### Motion

The mechanical choice is between moving the sample and moving the sensors. For detached grains, a turntable is mechanically simple, but vibration or rolling can change pose. A conveyor provides throughput but couples depth quality to speed and trigger timing. A robotic arm gives viewpoint flexibility but increases calibration and control dimensions.

For moving samples, the minimum state should include position, velocity, and acceleration. A simple proposed conveyor model is:

\[
p_{k+1}=p_k+T_s v_k,\qquad v_{k+1}=v_k+T_s a_k+w_k
\]

where \(T_s\) is the sampling period, \(a_k\) is the commanded or estimated acceleration, and \(w_k\) represents belt slip, vibration, and unmodeled disturbances. The model is intentionally simple; its parameters must be identified from encoder and image measurements.

The line-laser WG-3D system provides a useful design anchor because it combined a carrier table, servo drive, shaft encoder, timing belt, light-source controller, and line-scan camera. The carrier operated at 25 mm/s, and the camera generated valid point-cloud data while the carrier moved through the capture range [Wu et al., WG-3D](https://mdpi-res.com/d_attachment/agriculture/agriculture-12-01861/article_deploy/agriculture-12-01861-v4.pdf?version=1669083174). The system also completed the unseen grain bottom by projecting the point cloud to the carrier-table height. That step is computationally convenient but introduces a model-based assumption into volume and surface-area estimates.

### 2.4 State-space measurement model

The control system should model the instrument state rather than treating each image as an independent observation.

Let the state be

\[
x_k=[q_k,\dot{q}_k,T_{c,k},\omega_{c,k},\ell_k,e_k,f_k,\delta_k,\rho_k,\eta_k]^\top
\]

where \(q_k\) and \(\dot{q}_k\) describe stage or conveyor pose and velocity, \(T_{c,k}\) and \(\omega_{c,k}\) describe camera pose and angular velocity, \(\ell_k\) represents illumination state, \(e_k\) exposure and gain state, \(f_k\) focus state, \(\delta_k\) calibration or scale drift, \(\rho_k\) sample pose or motion, and \(\eta_k\) latent quality or reconstruction state. The exact state vector should be reduced after identifiability analysis.

Inputs may include:

\[
u_k=[u_{\mathrm{motion}},u_{\mathrm{camera}},u_{\mathrm{light}},u_{\mathrm{trigger}}]^\top
\]

Disturbances include vibration, belt slip, ambient-light drift, grain movement, temperature, and biological or surface variability. The general nonlinear stochastic state-space form is:

\[
x_{k+1}=f_k(x_k,u_k,v_k,\theta),\qquad y_k=h_k(x_k,u_k,e_k,\theta)
\]

This follows the state-space formulation of Schön, Wills, and Ninness, where \(x_k\) is the latent state, \(u_k\) the input, \(y_k\) the output, \(\theta\) the parameter vector, and \(v_k,e_k\) process and measurement disturbances [Schön, Wills, and Ninness](http://www.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2%3A400661/FULLTEXT01.pdf).

The measurement vector should combine physical and image observations:

\[
y_k=[y_{\mathrm{encoder}},y_{\mathrm{IMU}},y_{\mathrm{image}},y_{\mathrm{laser}},y_{\mathrm{quality}},y_{\mathrm{trait}}]^\top
\]

Examples of \(y_{\mathrm{quality}}\) include image sharpness, saturation fraction, feature-track count, stereo residual, structured-light correspondence rate, point density, visible-surface coverage, registration residual, segmentation confidence, and estimated trait uncertainty.

The grain geometry \(G\) should be treated as a latent object or parameter field, not automatically as a dynamic state. For a static detached grain, the observation model can be written as:

\[
I_{i,k}=\mathcal{P}_i(G,T_{i,k},\ell_k,e_k,\delta_k)+n_{i,k}
\]

where \(I_{i,k}\) is an image from sensor \(i\), \(\mathcal{P}_i\) is the projection and image-formation model, \(T_{i,k}\) is sensor pose, and \(n_{i,k}\) is image noise. If the experiment follows grain development over time, a biological growth state can be added, but such a model requires repeated observations and is not implied by detached-grain reconstruction.

The phenotype vector is then a function of geometry and segmentation:

\[
z_k=g(G_k,m_k,\mathcal{C}_k)
\]

where \(m_k\) is the instance or anatomical mask and \(\mathcal{C}_k\) contains coordinate conventions, mesh settings, and calibration parameters. This explicit separation makes it possible to distinguish uncertainty in image acquisition from uncertainty in geometry, segmentation, and trait definitions.

### 2.5 Data flow and quality gates

A robust data flow should contain at least six quality gates.

1. **Acquisition gate:** reject frames with saturation, blur, missing trigger, or insufficient exposure.
2. **Calibration gate:** verify intrinsic and extrinsic residuals, scale-board visibility, and stage-plane fit.
3. **Pose and coverage gate:** verify camera-pose convergence, overlap, visible-surface coverage, and motion consistency.
4. **Geometry gate:** test point density, outlier fraction, registration residual, mesh closure, and bottom completion.
5. **Segmentation gate:** test instance separation, connected-component plausibility, and mask confidence.
6. **Trait gate:** propagate uncertainty and flag traits whose confidence interval or geometry sensitivity exceeds the experiment’s declared limit.

The controller should not wait for a complete mesh before every decision. Fast proxies such as encoder error, image blur, illumination uniformity, feature-track count, laser return density, or partial-view coverage can be used in a fast loop. Complete reconstruction and phenotype uncertainty can update a slower loop.

## 3. Modern control-theoretic formulation and controller design

### 3.1 What should be controlled?

The instrument has several nested control problems.

#### Motion control

The low-level motion controller regulates conveyor speed, turntable angle, robotic-stage pose, and acceleration. Its feedback comes from encoders, motor current, inertial sensors, and limit switches.

#### Camera and optical control

The optical controller regulates focus, exposure, gain, trigger timing, projector intensity, laser power, and camera–sample distance. Its outputs are image sharpness, texture visibility, intensity uniformity, correspondence quality, and motion blur.

#### Information-quality control

The high-level controller decides whether the next action should continue, slow down, change viewpoint, change illumination, rescan, or reject the sample. Its objective is not merely a setpoint such as speed; it is sufficient geometric information with bounded uncertainty.

#### Throughput control

The system must balance quality against queue length and processing latency. A slower scan may improve reconstruction, but if reconstruction cannot keep up, memory and sample queues grow. Throughput is therefore a controlled resource.

A proposed quality vector is:

\[
q_k=[q_{\mathrm{blur}},q_{\mathrm{illum}},q_{\mathrm{overlap}},q_{\mathrm{coverage}},q_{\mathrm{density}},q_{\mathrm{seg}},q_{\mathrm{uncert}}]^\top
\]

The controller can regulate these variables toward acceptable regions rather than exact scalar setpoints.

### 3.2 System identification

Before controller synthesis, the instrument should be identified in the operating conditions where it will be used. The parameters \(\theta\) may include:

- motor gain, friction, and delay;
- conveyor speed and belt-slip dynamics;
- camera trigger delay;
- exposure and illumination response;
- focus response and depth-of-field behavior;
- motion-blur sensitivity to speed;
- reconstruction latency;
- point-density response to sample pose and illumination;
- segmentation confidence response to packing density; and
- trait sensitivity to calibration drift.

A safe identification experiment can vary one or more inputs over a bounded range while logging encoder position, timestamps, image quality, and reconstruction outputs. For example, stage velocity can be stepped or smoothly perturbed while image blur and point density are measured. Illumination can be varied over a safe range while feature-track count and segmentation quality are recorded.

For nonlinear state-space identification, Schön et al. describe maximum-likelihood estimation with an expectation–maximization procedure. The E-step uses nonlinear smoothed-state estimates, supplied by a particle smoother, and the M-step solves a numerical optimization problem. The framework is relevant because optical reconstruction residuals and segmentation confidence are not guaranteed to be Gaussian. The same authors warn that nonlinear prediction densities generally lack the closed-form integrals available to linear-Gaussian Kalman filtering and that likelihood optimization may contain multiple local minima [Schön, Wills, and Ninness](http://www.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2%3A400661/FULLTEXT01.pdf).

The identification dataset must therefore contain:

- raw inputs and actuator commands;
- sensor timestamps from a common clock;
- calibration version;
- environmental conditions;
- sample identity and cultivar;
- reconstruction method and software version;
- quality outputs;
- phenotype outputs; and
- operator interventions.

A model that predicts motor position but not acquisition latency is insufficient for closed-loop imaging. Likewise, a model that predicts point density on one cultivar but not under another illumination or moisture state is not a general phenotyping model.

### 3.3 State estimation

The controller needs an estimate of the current state, not merely the latest measurement.

#### Kalman and extended Kalman filtering

An extended Kalman filter (EKF) is appropriate when the system can be locally linearized and the disturbances are approximately Gaussian. It can estimate stage pose, velocity, camera pose, illumination drift, and calibration offsets from encoders, IMU data, image features, and quality metrics.

An unscented Kalman filter is preferable when first-order linearization is inadequate but the state dimension remains moderate. Both methods require reasonable process and measurement covariance models.

#### Particle filtering and smoothing

Particle methods are more appropriate when the posterior is multimodal. Typical causes include ambiguous feature matches, multiple possible sample poses, discontinuous segmentation hypotheses, and occlusion. The particle-smoothing approach described by Schön et al. is a transferable model-identification component, not a grain-specific benchmark.

A Bayesian reconstruction framework can be written as:

\[
p(G,x_{0:K},\theta\mid y_{0:K},u_{0:K})\propto p(y_{0:K}\mid G,x_{0:K},u_{0:K},\theta)p(G,x_{0:K},\theta)
\]

The prior may include calibrated scale, smoothness, symmetry, expected grain orientation, or a statistical shape model. Each prior must be declared because it can reduce variance while introducing biological or geometric bias.

#### Moving-horizon estimation

Moving-horizon estimation is useful when constraints matter. It can enforce feasible stage velocities, bounded illumination, and physically plausible pose changes while estimating states over a recent measurement window. It is computationally heavier than a Kalman filter but can be more robust to outliers and inequality constraints.

#### Multi-rate estimation

A practical estimator should operate at multiple rates:

- encoder and servo observations at the actuator rate;
- image-quality observations at the camera rate;
- partial geometric observations as frames arrive;
- full reconstruction observations when a sample or batch is complete.

The estimator should carry timestamps and covariance through all rates. A late reconstruction result must not be treated as if it were a current measurement.

### 3.4 Constrained model predictive control

MPC solves a finite-horizon optimization using the current estimated state, applies the first action, and repeats the optimization at the next sampling instant. The general structure is:

\[
\min_{u_{k:k+N-1}}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\left(\|q_{k+j}-q^\star\|_Q^2+\|\Delta u_{k+j}\|_R^2+\rho\,\phi_{k+j}\right)
\]

subject to the system dynamics, actuator limits, safety limits, and quality constraints. Here \(q^\star\) is a desired quality region, \(\Delta u\) penalizes aggressive changes, and \(\phi\) is a penalty for uncertainty, queue growth, or failed coverage.

A more complete proposed optimization is:

\[
\min \sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\left(\|q_{k+j}-q^\star\|_Q^2+\|\Delta u_{k+j}\|_R^2+\lambda_U U_{k+j}+\lambda_L L_{k+j}\right)
\]

where \(U_{k+j}\) is predicted phenotype uncertainty and \(L_{k+j}\) is reconstruction or processing latency. The controller can trade a slightly slower scan against a large reduction in trait uncertainty, provided the sample queue remains bounded.

Typical constraints include:

\[
u_{\min}\le u_k\le u_{\max},\quad \Delta u_{\min}\le\Delta u_k\le\Delta u_{\max},\quad q_k\in\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{safe}}
\]

The set \(\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{safe}}\) may require minimum image contrast, maximum blur, minimum visible-surface coverage, minimum point density, and maximum segmentation uncertainty.

The robust MPC formulation of [Campo and Morari](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Robust-Model-Predictive-Control-Campo-Morari/2166bbe723f45f5398924892bd4dfba46aa4e208) extends MPC to uncertain linear systems by minimizing worst-case tracking error over a family of models. Their linear-program reduction is conditional on an affine uncertainty description. For a grain-imaging stage, the affine uncertainty set would need to be identified from data rather than assumed.

The robust MPC with active disturbance rejection proposed for an underwater vehicle provides a useful architecture for the grain system. It augments the state with a total disturbance, estimates that disturbance through a discrete extended-state observer, and uses it to correct the first MPC action. The observer error matrix is designed with eigenvalues inside the unit circle, and the reported simulation reduced the disturbance-rejection integral-of-squared-error index to 24.75% of the ordinary MPC value. This is evidence for the transferable mechanism, not for grain-imaging performance [robust MPC–ADRC study](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-1312/11/5/929).

For a grain instrument, a disturbance observer could represent:

- belt-speed error;
- mechanical vibration;
- illumination drift;
- trigger delay;
- unmodeled focus response;
- sample motion;
- reconstruction latency; and
- systematic point-density loss.

The observer should not be allowed to absorb biological variation indiscriminately. A changed grain shape is not necessarily a disturbance to be rejected; it may be the phenotype of interest. The controller should distinguish instrument disturbances from sample-dependent measurement variation.

### 3.5 Adaptive and robust control

A fixed model may perform well for one grain type and fail for another because shape, reflectance, texture, and size alter the measurement response.

An adaptive controller can update parameters such as the motion-to-blur relationship, the illumination-to-feature-count relationship, or the latency model. Recursive least squares with covariance protection is a practical candidate for slowly changing actuator parameters. More complex Bayesian parameter estimation is appropriate when parameter uncertainty must be retained explicitly.

Adaptive control can become unsafe if it updates aggressively during a poorly observed event. The update should therefore be gated by:

- persistent excitation;
- residual consistency;
- parameter bounds;
- covariance reduction;
- absence of major segmentation failure; and
- agreement between independent sensors.

Sinha et al. propose adaptive robust MPC in which environmental uncertainty is learned online, matched uncertainty is treated with certainty-equivalent control, and remaining uncertainty is handled by tube MPC. Their guarantees target constraint satisfaction, recursive feasibility, and input-to-state stability under structural assumptions such as bounded features and linearly parameterizable unknown dynamics [Sinha et al.](https://stanfordasl.github.io/wp-content/papercite-data/pdf/Sinha.Harrison.ea.TAC21.pdf). Those assumptions must be checked before applying the method to imaging quality or biological variability.

For the proposed grain system, the recommended hierarchy is:

1. Use a nominal constrained MPC when the instrument operates inside a calibrated envelope.
2. Add a disturbance observer for repeatable vibration, timing, and illumination disturbances.
3. Use tube or min–max MPC when uncertainty bounds can be estimated.
4. Add adaptive parameter updates when operating conditions change slowly and persistently.
5. Fall back to a conservative scan, rescan, or stop state when the estimator loses observability.

### 3.6 Stability, controllability, observability, and identifiability

These properties should be analyzed before deployment. They should not be inferred from visually plausible reconstructions.

#### Local controllability

For a local discrete linearization,

\[
x_{k+1}=A x_k+B u_k,\qquad y_k=Cx_k
\]

the controllability matrix is:

\[
\mathcal{C}=[B\ AB\ A^2B\ \cdots\ A^{n-1}B]
\]

The local model is controllable if \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathcal{C})=n\). If stage speed, exposure, and focus are included in the state but no actuator can influence one of them within the relevant time horizon, the full model will not be controllable. That is not necessarily a failure; it may mean that the state should be separated into controllable and slowly drifting components.

#### Observability

The observability matrix is:

\[
\mathcal{O}=[C^\top\ (CA)^\top\ (CA^2)^\top\ \cdots\ (CA^{n-1})^\top]^\top
\]

The local model is observable if \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathcal{O})=n\). Camera pose, global scale, illumination, and surface reflectance may be confounded in passive imaging. An image sequence may identify relative pose but not absolute scale. A scale board, encoder, known working distance, or active depth measurement is therefore necessary to make the desired state observable.

Nonlinear observability should be checked with Lie-derivative rank tests or numerical observability Gramians. The test should be repeated for isolated grains, packed grains, dark grains, reflective grains, and partially occluded geometries.

#### Stability

At the estimator level, the discrete observer error dynamics must have poles inside the unit circle. The robust MPC–ADRC literature uses this criterion for convergence under bounded disturbance-rate assumptions [robust MPC–ADRC study](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-1312/11/5/929).

At the closed-loop level, the proposed MPC should use a terminal cost, terminal set, or another recursively feasible design if formal stability is required. The analysis should include input saturation, computation delay, dropped frames, delayed phenotype updates, and fallback behavior.

A sufficient engineering test is to verify that:

- the optimizer remains feasible over the operating envelope;
- the queue remains bounded;
- state-estimation residuals remain within declared bounds;
- constrained trajectories do not violate motion or optical limits;
- the closed-loop error remains bounded under the identified disturbance set; and
- the fallback controller is stable when the high-level optimizer fails.

No crop-grain-specific stability benchmark was supplied. These are required pre-deployment analyses.

#### Structural identifiability

Structural identifiability asks whether unknown parameters can, in principle, be recovered from the chosen inputs and outputs. Cobelli and Romanin-Jacur formulated controllability, observability, and structural identifiability for biological compartmental systems to assess the a priori possibility of estimating unknown parameters in a multi-input, multi-output experiment [Cobelli and Romanin-Jacur](https://doi.org/10.1109/tbme.1976.324568).

For the imaging instrument, candidate parameters may include scale, baseline, lens distortion, trigger delay, illumination gain, conveyor slip, and motion-blur coefficients. If different parameter combinations produce indistinguishable image and encoder outputs, no optimizer can recover them uniquely.

A practical local test uses the sensitivity matrix:

\[
S_{ij}=\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial\theta_j}
\]

and information matrix:

\[
\mathcal{I}_\theta=S^\top R^{-1}S
\]

where \(R\) is the measurement-noise covariance. A poorly conditioned or rank-deficient \(\mathcal{I}_\theta\) indicates confounding. The experiment should then add a new input or sensor rather than merely collect more repetitions of the same uninformative motion.

### 3.7 Multi-rate implementation and delay management

The controller must account for the fact that image acquisition, reconstruction, segmentation, and trait extraction have different time scales.

A proposed initial implementation, to be measured rather than assumed, is:

- a 100–500 Hz inner servo loop for motor position or velocity;
- a 10–30 Hz image-quality loop for blur, illumination, feature density, and triggering;
- a 5–20 Hz MPC loop for motion and acquisition-quality decisions;
- an event-based reconstruction loop operating when a view set or grain is complete; and
- a slower experiment-level adaptation loop for cultivar, moisture, or environmental changes.

The exact frequencies should be chosen from identified actuator bandwidth and reconstruction delay. A controller operating at 10 Hz cannot safely use a phenotype estimate that arrives several seconds later without modeling that delay. In the presence of long latency, the fast loop should use immediate quality proxies and the slow loop should update scan policy or rescan decisions.

A simple timing requirement is:

\[
T_{\mathrm{capture}}+T_{\mathrm{transfer}}+T_{\mathrm{reconstruct}}+T_{\mathrm{segment}}+T_{\mathrm{trait}}\le T_{\mathrm{available}}
\]

where \(T_{\mathrm{available}}\) is the time before the sample reaches the next physical decision point. If the inequality cannot be met, the system should decouple acquisition from analysis, buffer the sample identity, and use delayed feedback for the next sample rather than pretending that feedback is real time.

## 4. Complementary reconstruction, estimation, optimization, and shape models

### 4.1 Reconstruction as an inverse problem

The measurement process can be represented abstractly as:

\[
y=\mathcal{F}(G,\xi,\theta)+\varepsilon
\]

where \(G\) is the unknown grain geometry, \(\xi\) contains pose and illumination states, \(\theta\) contains calibration and model parameters, and \(\varepsilon\) is measurement noise. Reconstruction seeks an estimate \(\hat{G}\) from incomplete and noisy observations.

Because the problem is often ill-posed, the estimate should be expressed as an optimization or posterior rather than as an unquestionable object:

\[
\hat{G}=\arg\min_G\left[\|y-\mathcal{F}(G,\hat{\xi},\hat{\theta})\|_{R^{-1}}^2+\lambda\mathcal{R}(G)\right]
\]

The regularizer \(\mathcal{R}(G)\) may encode smoothness, surface continuity, symmetry, shape-model plausibility, or agreement between modalities. Each regularizer changes the bias–variance trade-off.

### 4.2 Modality-specific reconstruction branches

#### SfM–MVS

SfM estimates camera poses and a sparse point cloud from overlapping images; MVS then densifies the result. The workflow can include SIFT, ORB, or SURF features, robust matching, RANSAC, triangulation, bundle adjustment, and dense stereo. The principal strengths are low hardware cost, color preservation, and flexible camera placement. The main weaknesses are weak texture, reflective surfaces, insufficient overlap, motion, and processing time.

The 2018 maize comparison showed that MVS outperformed 3D laser scanning for small V5 plants because thin leaves moved during the longer scanning process. At later stages, tall maize plants generated upper-part deviations when MVS required multiple image layers [Wang et al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/rs11010063). The result illustrates that modality superiority is conditional on object scale and motion stability.

#### Structured light and line laser

Structured light provides dense correspondence through controlled patterns. Line-laser stereo provides a strong depth cue along a moving scan line and is naturally compatible with encoder-synchronized conveyors. Both methods require careful calibration and controlled illumination.

The cereal-grain structured-light workflow combined greedy projection triangulation, mesh-boundary repair, and convex-pentahedron volume construction. It measured 2,000 rice grains, 100 wheat grains, and 100 corn grains against micrometer measurements from three experimenters. Across 2,200 samples, length, width, and thickness MAPE values were 2.07%, 0.97%, and 1.13%, with \(R^2\) values of 0.9940, 0.9960, and 0.9960 [Qin et al.](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-07221-4).

#### 3D Gaussian Splatting and NeRF

3DGS represents a scene using explicit Gaussian primitives with position, covariance, opacity, and appearance. The seed study initialized Gaussians from an SfM cloud and optimized them using a photometric loss combining \(L_1\) and SSIM terms, with \(\lambda=0.2\). At 7,000 iterations its reported average reconstruction time was 694 seconds, compared with 757 seconds for SfM–MVS; at 30,000 iterations it required 1,744 seconds and produced a denser representation. These times are reported as average reconstruction times in the study and should not be treated as a universal per-grain timing benchmark [Agriculture (2025) seed study](https://doi.org/10.3390/agriculture15222329).

For Zhengdan 958 maize seeds, the same study reported 3DGS \(R^2\) values of 0.9361, 0.8889, and 0.946 for length, width, and height, compared with 0.812, 0.777, and 0.8917 for MVS. The 3DGS MAPE values were 1.91%, 3.99%, and 3.66%; MVS values were 2.97%, 4.35%, and 5.76%. These results support the method as a promising external-geometry branch, but the sample and cultivars do not establish performance for all grain morphologies.

NeRF and 3DGS should be treated as reconstruction representations rather than phenotype definitions. PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS evaluate rendered-image fidelity. They do not directly guarantee correct length, thickness, curvature, surface area, or volume. The plant-reconstruction literature explicitly warns that neural-rendering realism should not be conflated with phenotype accuracy for thin organs, texture-poor surfaces, motion, and changing illumination [3D reconstruction review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13165976/).

#### CT

CT produces a volumetric voxel representation from multi-angle X-ray projections. Surface and internal masks can then be extracted with thresholding, region growing, U-Net segmentation, connected components, and Marching Cubes.

The 2023 maize-kernel pipeline trained a 2D U-Net with a VGG16 backbone using 428 images from 30 kernel scans. It reported 97.6% Dice accuracy. On 48 manually segmented kernels, \(R^2\) values for silty endosperm, embryo, endosperm cavity, endosperm, and embryo cavity volumes were 0.77, 0.95, 0.94, 0.95, and 0.73, respectively. Lower performance for small structures illustrates why a high segmentation score does not imply equal accuracy for every trait.

CT resolution must be selected for useful biological information, not for the smallest available voxel. A wheat-spike study found that increasing resolution from 68.8 µm to 34.4 µm increased scan time from approximately 40 to 60 minutes without improving routine grain-trait output; a 17.2 µm setting required approximately 3.3 hours and produced a 32 GB dataset [Plant Methods (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13007-017-0229-8).

### 4.3 Point-cloud processing and segmentation

The reconstruction branch should produce both a geometry object and a processing provenance record.

A typical external pipeline is:

1. denoise statistically or with a learned denoiser;
2. downsample only after recording the original density;
3. fit and remove the carrier plane using RANSAC;
4. separate instances using Euclidean clustering, region growing, density clustering, or a learned instance model;
5. align each grain to a declared coordinate system;
6. repair or reconstruct the surface;
7. compute traits and uncertainty.

The 2025 3DGS seed pipeline used statistical-neighbor filtering, voxel-grid downsampling, RANSAC plane fitting, and Euclidean Cluster Extraction. The Sensors seed system combined RANSAC, region growing, dimensional-feature detection, PCA normalization, ellipse-based completion, and Poisson reconstruction [Sensors (2024)](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/24/18/6117).

When point clouds are incomplete, completion must be recorded as a model assumption. The Sensors system divided a single-seed point cloud into 20 sections along one axis, fitted ellipses to incomplete profiles, and filled missing points before Poisson reconstruction. This was reported as useful for irregular broad beans, peanuts, and kidney beans, but it remains a shape prior rather than a direct observation.

Packed grains require a distinction between semantic segmentation and instance separation. Image segmentation provides color and texture semantics but does not inherently resolve occlusion. Point-cloud segmentation uses spatial separation but may lack semantic information. The rice VRKGNet system addressed this by projecting 2D image labels into a 3D cloud and fusing them with point-cloud features; it reported semantic mIoU of 88.79% and instance AP25 of 84.55% in rice plant scenes [Fine-grained 3D rice phenotyping](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13316263/). This is a transferable multimodal strategy, but its plant-scale performance should not be reported as grain-instance accuracy.

For deep point-cloud segmentation, downsampling is itself a design variable. A cross-evaluation of five samplers and five segmentation networks found no universal best sampler. Random sampling was fastest but sensitive to original density; farthest-point sampling improved global coverage but could be computationally expensive; voxel methods were fast but required tuned voxel size; and edge-preserving methods retained boundaries at the cost of additional tuning [Plant Methods point-cloud sampling study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10640751/).

### 4.4 Statistical shape models and geometric morphometrics

#### PCA and statistical shape models

PCA of point coordinates or mesh vertices provides a practical size-and-pose model. If \(X_i\) is a vectorized aligned shape, a statistical shape model can be written as:

\[
X_i=\bar{X}+\Phi b_i+\epsilon_i
\]

where \(\bar{X}\) is the mean shape, \(\Phi\) contains principal directions, \(b_i\) are specimen scores, and \(\epsilon_i\) is residual variation. PCA is useful for pose normalization, outlier detection, low-dimensional regression, and missing-shape completion.

However, PCA axes are geometric. In the 2026 wheat-kernel CT dataset, the principal-axis lengths were ordered \(L_1\ge L_2\ge L_3\), but the authors explicitly warned that the axes are not guaranteed to correspond to anatomical directions [Shi et al.](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-07207-1).

#### Geometric morphometrics

Geometric morphometrics preserves spatial relationships among landmarks, semilandmarks, or surface coordinates. Procrustes superimposition removes translation, rotation, and scale before shape analysis. Semilandmarks can describe curves and surfaces, while Fourier and eigenshape methods can describe outlines.

The plant GMM review by Spani, Locato, and De Gara found 83 studies, but only 7 used 3D landmarks and only 2 addressed seeds. Most of the literature concerned leaves and flowers rather than grains [Spani et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2223-7747/14/5/808). This is important evidence for the method’s relevance, but also a warning against claiming a mature grain-specific 3D GMM standard.

A defensible grain GMM design should use biologically meaningful landmarks where available:

- germ or embryo attachment;
- crease endpoints;
- dorsal and ventral extrema;
- proximal and distal tips;
- shoulder or crown features;
- anatomical boundaries visible in CT.

Where discrete homology is not defensible, semilandmarks or surface correspondence should be used with explicit sensitivity analysis. Automated surface-only methods can be unstable when principal axes are similar or when shape differences are weakly localized; simulation work comparing landmark and surface-only methods found that landmarks plus semilandmarks and one surface method most consistently recovered known shape differences [Eovito, Glynne, and Adams](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11692-026-09674-1).

The shape-analysis objective should be separated from dimensional measurement. PCA or OBB dimensions answer “how large and elongated is the grain?” Procrustes or surface morphometrics answer “how does the form differ after size and pose are removed?” A cultivar or stress effect may appear in one space but not the other.

### 4.5 Bayesian uncertainty and state estimation

Uncertainty enters at several levels:

- image intensity and correspondence;
- camera pose and calibration;
- scale;
- point coordinates;
- segmentation;
- completion of unseen surfaces;
- mesh reconstruction;
- trait definitions;
- biological sampling.

The measurement model for a reconstructed point can be written as:

\[
x_i=x(u_i,v_i)+\epsilon_i
\]

with:

\[
\epsilon_i=\epsilon_i^{\mathrm{random}}+\epsilon_i^{\mathrm{systematic}}
\]

The 2026 surface-metrology study identifies sensor noise, calibration error, environmental influence, and acquisition limitations as uncertainty sources. It also warns that curvature depends on second-order derivatives, so small coordinate perturbations can produce large curvature deviations [Metrology (2026)](https://doi.org/10.3390/metrology6020043).

For a locally linear trait transformation \(t=g(p)\), a first-order covariance approximation is:

\[
\Sigma_t\approx J_g\Sigma_pJ_g^\top
\]

This is useful for dimensions and simple ratios near a well-behaved operating point. It is insufficient for strongly nonlinear operations such as surface completion, segmentation thresholds, mesh closure, curvature, or ratios near zero.

Monte Carlo propagation is therefore preferred for high-sensitivity traits:

1. sample calibration, point, segmentation, and completion errors from their declared distributions;
2. reconstruct or perturb the geometry;
3. recompute the trait;
4. repeat sufficiently many times;
5. report the median, bias, standard deviation, percentile interval, and covariance with other traits.

The metrology study used synthetic spherical, cylindrical, and free-form surfaces and found nonlinear curvature uncertainty growth with coordinate noise. In its particular fixed-neighborhood simulation, increasing point density at constant coordinate noise increased curvature uncertainty because the effective spatial fitting window became smaller. This is not a universal law that denser sampling is worse; it demonstrates that density, smoothing, neighborhood size, and noise must be analyzed jointly.

Lai et al. provide a transferable Bayesian reconstruction perspective by combining empirical Bayes modeling with MCMC filters for uncertainty quantification from noisy 2D pixels. Their application was cryo-electron microscopy and infant brain development, not grains, so the method should be treated as a general uncertainty framework rather than grain evidence [Lai et al.](https://www3.stat.sinica.edu.tw/statistica/oldpdf/A33n2129.pdf).

## 5. 3D grain-phenotype catalogue, uncertainty, and validation

### 5.1 Trait definitions

The system should publish a phenotype dictionary before collecting a large experiment. Every trait must include a name, unit, coordinate convention, algorithm version, mask definition, and uncertainty field.

| Trait | Operational definition | Representation and convention | Biological or engineering use | Principal caveat |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Length | Largest principal or declared anatomical extent | \(L_1\), the largest OBB/PCA dimension, or tip-to-tip anatomical distance | Grain size, filling, cultivar and stress comparison | PCA length is geometric and may not equal anatomical length |
| Width | Intermediate transverse extent | \(L_2\), measured orthogonal to the length axis | Size, shape, packing, milling-related analysis | Sensitive to pose, incomplete sides, and crease boundaries |
| Thickness | Smallest principal extent | \(L_3\), measured orthogonal to the first two axes | Kernel fullness and flattening | Often most sensitive to occlusion and depth noise |
| Volume | Volume enclosed by a closed surface or occupied voxels | Mesh tetrahedral sum, Alpha Shape, voxel count, or CT mask | Filling, density when combined with mass, internal component ratios | Bottom completion and mesh closure can dominate error |
| Surface area | Area of the reconstructed external surface | Sum of triangle areas or Marching-Cubes surface | Surface-to-volume ratio, shrivelling, texture and processing analysis | Independent irregular-grain ground truth is not established |
| Gaussian curvature | Product of principal curvatures | \(K=(LN-M^2)/(EG-F^2)\) from a fitted surface | Local concavity, crease, tip, and surface-form analysis | Second-order derivatives amplify noise |
| Mean curvature | Mean of principal curvatures | \(H=(EN-2FM+GL)/(2(EG-F^2))\) | Local bending and surface regularity | Depends strongly on smoothing scale and neighborhood |
| Sphericity | Surface compactness relative to a sphere of equal volume | \(\psi=\pi^{1/3}(6V)^{2/3}/A\), if this convention is declared | Roundness and filling-related shape | Formula and treatment of rough surfaces must be fixed |
| Aspect ratio | Ratio of two declared dimensions | Report \(AR_{12}=L_1/L_2\) and, if needed, \(AR_{23}=L_2/L_3\) | Elongation and flattening | No single universal grain-specific definition was established |
| Elongation index | Width-to-length ratio | \(EI=L_2/L_1\) | Shape independent of absolute size | Inverse of a common length-to-width aspect ratio |
| Flatness index | Thickness-to-width ratio | \(FI=L_3/L_2\) | Flattening and kernel form | Geometric, not necessarily anatomical |
| Convexity | Object volume relative to convex-hull volume | \(C_v=V_p/V_h\) | Concavity, crease, and shrivelling | Sensitive to hull construction and outliers |
| Cross-sectional area and perimeter | Area and boundary length of a declared section | Orthogonal or anatomically aligned slice | Local shape and orientation analysis | Section location must be reproducible |
| Shape coordinates | Aligned landmark, semilandmark, contour, or surface coordinates | Procrustes, Fourier, eigenshape, or SSM scores | Cultivar, stress, developmental and genetic analysis | Homology and correspondence may be uncertain |

The sphericity convention above is a standard geometric definition, but a study must declare it explicitly because the supplied grain studies use the term without a single common implementation. The Sensors seed study grouped volume, surface area, length, width, thickness, cross-sectional perimeter, and cross-sectional area as size-related phenotypes, and roundness, needle degree, flatness, shape factor, sphericity, elongation, circularity, and compactness as shape-related phenotypes [Sensors (2024)](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/24/18/6117).

The aspect-ratio field remains particularly vulnerable to ambiguity. The strongest supported partial answer is to report the two independent ratios \(L_1/L_2\) and \(L_2/L_3\), together with the reciprocal elongation and flatness indices. A paper should not report “aspect ratio” without naming the numerator, denominator, axis convention, and whether dimensions are PCA-derived, OBB-derived, or anatomical.

### 5.2 Evidence for external grain traits

The literature gives several useful but non-identical validation anchors.

#### Wheat

The structured-light wheat study used 125 grains from five commercial varieties and compared length, width, and thickness against manual values. Structured-light \(R^2\) values were 0.8705, 0.8046, and 0.8836, with RMSE values of 0.149, 0.076, and 0.080 mm and MAPE values of 1.83%, 1.86%, and 2.19%. CT produced higher \(R^2\) values but similar RMSE and MAPE. This disagreement demonstrates why ranking modalities by \(R^2\) alone is unsafe.

The same workflow extracted 32 traits from 500 grains and used regression models to estimate single-grain weight. Gradient boosting achieved \(R^2=0.8345\), MAPE 3.37%, and RMSE 2.45 mg under tenfold cross-validation [Frontiers wheat study](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/plant-science/articles/10.3389/fpls.2022.840908/full). That result concerns a prediction task, not direct geometric accuracy.

The line-laser WG-3D system validated 100 grains each from three wheat varieties and tested 40 grains from each of 26 Yangmai-series varieties. It reported length RMSE 0.2256 mm and MAPE 2.60%, width RMSE 0.2154 mm and MAPE 5.83%, thickness RMSE 0.2119 mm and MAPE 5.81%, and volume RMSE 1.7740 mm³ and MAPE 4.31% [Wu et al.](https://mdpi-res.com/d_attachment/agriculture/agriculture-12-01861/article_deploy/agriculture-12-01861-v4.pdf?version=1669083174).

A 2026 CT dataset released surface models and slice stacks for 100 Jimai 22 wheat kernels and extracted principal-axis lengths, elongation, flatness, convexity, and sphericity. Its sample was intentionally restricted to intact, uniformly plump kernels from one source batch at 10.2% wet-basis moisture, so it does not establish robustness for shrivelled, diseased, damaged, or stress-deformed kernels [Shi et al.](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-07207-1).

#### Rice, wheat, and maize

The structured-light cereal-grain study used 2,000 rice, 100 wheat, and 100 corn grains. Across the combined sample, length, width, and thickness MAPE values were 2.07%, 0.97%, and 1.13%. Vertical placement improved the rice result, showing that mechanical presentation is part of the measurement system, not merely sample preparation [Qin et al.](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-07221-4).

The 2025 3DGS study used 50 seeds from each of six cultivars: Zhengdan 958 and Tianguinuo 932 maize, Jimai 22 and Aikang 58 wheat, and Suijing 18 and Xiangya Xiangzhan rice. Its length, width, and height \(R^2\) values were generally above 0.84, but rice width and height errors were larger. For Xiangya Xiangzhan, width and height MAPE values were 9.63% and 9.10%; for Suijing 18, height MAPE was 8.34%. This is a practical example of domain shift within a multi-crop experiment: good average reconstruction does not imply equal accuracy for slender dimensions [Agriculture (2025) seed study](https://doi.org/10.3390/agriculture15222329).

The wheat-seed deep-learning study reported that conventional volume carving required approximately 36 images and 20 seconds, while a three-image neural method reduced imaging time by a factor of ten and produced relative errors around 2% for volume, length, width, and height. The output was described as an approximate point cloud, so the result supports fast screening but does not validate high-fidelity surface curvature or area [Deep learning based 3D reconstruction for phenotyping of wheat seeds](https://doi.org/10.1109/iccvw60793.2023.00063).

### 5.3 Internal traits and stress-related phenotypes

CT supports traits that optical external imaging cannot observe. In the maize-kernel CT study, the 20-trait catalogue included kernel length, width, thickness, volume, area, specific surface area, sphericity, embryo volume and ratio, endosperm volume and ratios, and several cavity measures. Cavity traits showed substantially greater variability than basic dimensions, which makes them potentially informative but also more sensitive to segmentation and noise [Agronomy maize CT study](https://doi.org/10.3390/agronomy13041078).

The 3DPheno-Seed&Fruit pipeline extracted length, width, thickness, radius, surface area, volume, compactness, and sphericity from CT images. Against repeated micrometer measurements, wheat seeds showed \(R^2\) values of 0.96, 0.89, 0.81, and 0.91 for length, width, thickness, and radius, respectively. The corresponding MAPE values were 1.74%, 3.30%, 3.20%, and 2.62% [3DPheno-Seed&Fruit](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7688911/).

For biological interpretation, CT-derived morphology can reveal stress mechanisms rather than merely classify samples. In wheat ears exposed to drought versus combined drought and heat, mean seed volume was 23.04 mm³ under drought and 7.98 mm³ under combined stress, while spherical ratio declined from 0.53 to 0.46. The combined treatment produced smaller, less round seeds and more shrivelled forms, while mean attenuation was 0.80 under both treatments [Plant Methods wheat CT study](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13007-020-00565-w). The observed association supports a plausible grain-filling mechanism, but it should not be generalized across cultivars or environments without external validation.

### 5.4 Validation hierarchy

A validation study should separate algorithmic correctness, metric accuracy, repeatability, reproducibility, and biological generalization.

| Validation question | Reference or design | Recommended metrics | Supported evidence anchor | Interpretation limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Does the geometry algorithm work? | Ceramic ball, calibrated sphere, or reference artifact | Diameter, area, volume error | Ceramic-ball diameter error 0.0223 mm; 3DGS sphere area and volume errors 1.67% and 1.14% | Regular objects do not validate irregular-grain completion |
| Are dimensions accurate? | Three repeated micrometer or caliper measurements by independent operators | Bias, RMSE, MAPE, \(R^2\), Bland–Altman limits | Qin et al. used three experimenters and thousands of grains; wheat structured light used manual references | Manual dimensions do not establish surface-area or curvature truth |
| Is external geometry complete? | Independent CT, high-precision scanner, or registered reference model | Chamfer distance, Hausdorff distance, coverage, missing-surface fraction | Crop studies use CT or reference point clouds for comparison | Cross-modality comparison is not automatically ground truth |
| Is the algorithm repeatable? | Same grain, same operator, repeated acquisition and reconstruction | Within-run SD, CV, ICC, trait covariance | Grain-specific cross-run benchmarks remain unavailable in the supplied evidence | Must include re-mounting and recalibration |
| Is it reproducible? | Different days, operators, instruments, and software versions | Between-run and between-instrument variance, ICC, agreement limits | No complete crop-grain benchmark was retrieved | Requires a pre-registered protocol |
| Does it generalize biologically? | Held-out cultivars, species, moisture, stress, year, packing, and illumination | External RMSE/MAPE, calibration slope, uncertainty coverage | OSTRA plant-height \(R^2\) declined from 0.97 within condition to 0.72 cross-year | Plant-scale validation does not establish grain-scale generalization |

A sphere is useful for testing triangulation, mesh closure, area computation, and volume integration. Qin et al. used a 10 mm-radius sphere because direct non-destructive measurement of irregular grain surface area and volume was difficult; the reported errors were 2.83% for area and 1.75% for volume [Qin et al.](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-07221-4). The 3DGS study used a sphere of approximately 22 mm diameter and reported 1.67% surface-area error and 1.14% volume error [Agriculture (2025) seed study](https://doi.org/10.3390/agriculture15222329). These values validate the computational pipeline on regular objects, not the biological grain surface.

For irregular grains, independent ground truth for surface area and volume remains unavailable in the supplied evidence. The strongest supported partial answer is therefore a tiered validation strategy: use artifacts for algorithm verification, manual dimensions for primary metric validation, CT or a higher-precision reference for selected specimens, and repeatability studies for uncertainty characterization.

### 5.5 Uncertainty reporting

Every reported trait should include at least:

- point estimate and unit;
- method and representation;
- sample-level quality flag;
- calibration version;
- segmentation confidence;
- uncertainty interval;
- number of Monte Carlo or bootstrap realizations;
- covariance with related traits where relevant;
- missing-surface or completion fraction; and
- whether uncertainty is random, systematic, model-based, or biological.

For a mesh-derived volume, uncertainty should include segmentation perturbation, mesh-reconstruction settings, hole-filling policy, scale uncertainty, and the effect of downsampling. For curvature, the fitting neighborhood and smoothing scale are part of the measurand definition; changing them changes the trait.

A trait should be marked unavailable rather than assigned a numerical value when the mesh is open, the bottom is entirely unobserved without a defensible prior, segmentation is ambiguous, or the uncertainty distribution is unbounded or multimodal. This is preferable to silently treating a completed surface as observed geometry.

Uncertainty visualization can use per-point or per-face confidence maps, but a single scalar summary may also be useful. A volume-weighted uncertainty formula has been proposed in another 3D reconstruction domain:

\[
AU_V=\frac{\sum_i Vol_i\,Uncert_i}{\sum_i Vol_i}
\]

The formula is segmentation-invariant when valid closed volumes are preserved, but it was developed for hypothetical architectural reconstruction, not grain metrology [Apollonio, Fallavollita, and Foschi](https://www.mdpi.com/2571-9408/7/8/209). For grains, it could be adapted only as a declared summary of completion or source confidence; it should not replace coordinate-level covariance or trait-level Monte Carlo uncertainty.

### 5.6 Biological interpretation and genetic analysis

Phenotype extraction is not the same as biological inference. A change in volume may result from grain filling, moisture, cultivar, orientation bias, or segmentation. A change in curvature may represent a true crease difference or a smoothing artifact.

The maize CT study illustrates a useful downstream workflow: 303 inbred lines, 20 kernel traits, and GWAS identified 26 significant SNPs and 62 candidate genes for selected embryo, endosperm, and cavity traits. This demonstrates that 3D traits can enter genetic analysis, but the reported associations still require biological validation and should not be interpreted as causal from morphology alone [Agronomy maize CT study](https://doi.org/10.3390/agronomy13041078).

Similarly, OSTRA reconstructed 231 rice landraces and derived plant height, leaf area, and panicle length for GWAS. Within-condition plant-height validation was \(R^2=0.97\), but cross-year validation with manual data yielded \(R^2=0.72\) for plant height and \(R^2=0.80\) for panicle length [OSTRA](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13007-026-01499-5). The result shows why external biological validation must accompany high within-condition accuracy.

## 6. Integrated experimental and implementation design

### 6.1 Three operating configurations

A practical research program should build one common data and control architecture with three interchangeable sensing configurations.

| Operating objective | Preferred configuration | Why it is appropriate | Main unresolved issue | Control emphasis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| High-throughput external traits of isolated grains | Conveyor or turntable with structured light or line-laser stereo | Direct metric depth, strong dimensional accuracy, controllable illumination | Bottom visibility, surface reflectance, calibration drift | Speed, trigger timing, coverage, blur, and rescan decisions |
| Low-cost portable screening | Smartphone or calibrated multi-camera MVS, optionally 3DGS | Low hardware cost, color preservation, flexible deployment | Scale, sparse views, textureless surfaces, computational cost | Viewpoint planning, overlap, exposure, and adaptive frame selection |
| Internal anatomy and reference validation | X-ray micro-CT | Complete volumetric coverage and internal component segmentation | Scan time, memory, cost, radiation-management procedures, segmentation | Scan protocol, reconstruction quality, queue scheduling, and CT reference selection |

Structured light or line-laser stereo should be the primary platform for a large external-grain study. MVS or 3DGS should be used for portability, rapid screening, or experiments where the color and visual representation are valuable. CT should be used for all internal-trait studies and for a deliberately selected reference subset in external-trait validation.

### 6.2 Mechanical and optical specification

The proposed initial instrument should include:

- a matte, replaceable sample carrier;
- controlled slots or shallow pockets that constrain grain movement without masking the measurement surface;
- an encoder on every moving axis;
- a rigid camera and projector frame;
- an enclosure with diffuse, controllable illumination;
- an image-level brightness and blur monitor;
- a calibration board or reference artifact visible at the working distance;
- a synchronized hardware trigger;
- a temperature and humidity logger;
- a reject or rescan position; and
- a common timestamp distributed to motion, camera, lighting, and reconstruction processes.

The starting geometry should be treated as an experimental factor rather than a permanent setting. The wheat structured-light study supports testing a 30° turntable rotation and 37° scan angle. The cereal-grain study supports testing 45° turntable steps. The binocular analysis supports testing optical-axis/baseline angles within 25°–60°, with focused testing around 40°–50°. These values should be evaluated using the target grain size, camera resolution, working distance, and desired trait uncertainty.

The line-laser system should begin near the reported 25 mm/s carrier speed only if the camera line rate, laser exposure, and required point spacing are comparable. The speed must be recalculated from the desired along-track sampling interval:

\[
f_{\mathrm{line}}=\frac{v_{\mathrm{carrier}}}{\Delta s_{\mathrm{along-track}}}
\]

A faster conveyor is not automatically higher throughput if the resulting point spacing increases thickness or curvature error.

### 6.3 Calibration protocol

Calibration should be separated into four layers.

#### Camera calibration

Estimate focal length, principal point, distortion, and relative pose. The calibration target should occupy the same working region as the grains. The 2025 wheat line-scan system used a honeycomb plate with 5 mm dots and checked roundness and aspect ratio above 0.95 at different tray positions [Applied Sciences (2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/15/10/5484).

#### Metric scale

Passive reconstruction requires scale recovery. The 3DGS seed study used a 10 cm × 10 cm board with 6 mm × 6 mm black squares and applied \(P=L_{\mathrm{real}}/L_{\mathrm{model}}\) to reconstructed coordinates [Agriculture (2025) seed study](https://doi.org/10.3390/agriculture15222329). The proposed system should retain the original board geometry, image observations, fitted scale, and residual rather than storing only the final scale factor.

#### Stage and plane calibration

Fit the carrier or turntable plane with RANSAC and record its residual. The plane should be checked at multiple positions to identify tilt, sag, or vibration. If bottom completion uses the plane, its uncertainty must be propagated into volume and area.

#### Temporal calibration

Measure the delay between encoder position, trigger command, sensor exposure, and image arrival. Timestamp alignment errors become spatial errors on a moving conveyor. If the sample moves at velocity \(v\) and the total unmodeled delay is \(\Delta t\), the first-order positional error is \(v\Delta t\).

Calibration should be performed at the start of every acquisition session and after a mechanical, optical, temperature, or software change. A fast reference scan should also be inserted between blocks of samples.

### 6.4 Acquisition and computation timing

Reported systems demonstrate a wide range of timing:

- the structured-light wheat workflow required approximately 5 minutes for 25 grains, or about 12 seconds per grain, including scans and processing;
- the Qin et al. cereal-grain system required approximately 4 minutes for 25 grains, or 9.6 seconds per grain;
- WG-3D required approximately 12 seconds for scanning and 3.18 seconds for processing per grain at 25 mm/s;
- conventional wheat-seed volume carving used approximately 36 images and 20 seconds of acquisition;
- the maize CT pipeline extracted 20 traits within 5 seconds after CT image acquisition;
- CT wheat-spike scans required approximately 7 minutes per ear in one throughput description, with another methods description reporting approximately 27 minutes per scan;
- 3DGS seed reconstruction times ranged from 624 to 1,744 seconds in the reported comparison, but the study’s timing unit is an average reconstruction time rather than a universal per-grain production rate.

These values are not directly comparable because they include different combinations of acquisition, reconstruction, segmentation, batch size, hardware, and object scale. They are nevertheless useful for constructing a timing budget.

A proposed timing architecture is:

- hard real-time servo and trigger control;
- asynchronous image transfer;
- immediate quality screening;
- GPU reconstruction in a bounded worker queue;
- trait extraction after geometry completion;
- delayed quality feedback to the next sample or next scan segment; and
- hard queue and memory limits that force a slower scan or temporary stop.

The controller should use the fastest reliable signal available. A complete surface-area estimate may arrive too late to control the current grain, whereas blur, encoder error, laser return, and feature coverage can be available immediately.

### 6.5 Experimental design

A minimum external-validation experiment should block by:

- species: wheat, rice, maize;
